newsitem.title: GERMANY: German Bundesbank says 1996 profits fall.
newsitem.headline: German Bundesbank says 1996 profits fall.

text.p: Germany's Bundesbank said on Thursday its 1996 profits fell compared to the year before with the central bank making a 9.43 billion mark profit on its operations compared to 10.93 billion marks in 1995.
The figure was within economists' expectations of profit dropping to between eight and 10 billion marks as a result of the bank's reduction in interest rates last year to historic lows.
Like other central banks, the Bundesbank makes money by lending to commercial banks.

Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer told a news conference that the lower profits would mean that, minus payments into reserves, the bank would contribute 8.83 billion marks into federal government funds compared to 10.32 billion in 1995.

While such a fall is no help in Germany's attempt to cut state deficits for entry into European monetary union in 1999, the amount of shortfall involved is slight compared to a public sector deficit expected to top 100 billion marks this year.
Interest income totalled 12.9 billion marks against 1995's total of 15.1 billion marks. Some 6.6 billion of last year's figure came from international transactions.
Expenses, including the cost of printing banknotes, also fell to 3.9 billion marks from 4.7 billion largely as a result of lower write-downs of monetary reserves.

Its balance sheet total rose 12.0 billion marks to 366.4 billion. A 13 billion mark rise in assets on lending to domestic institutions was largely offset by a 12 billion mark gain in liabilities linked to an increase in the number of banknotes in circulation.
Tietmeyer told the news conference that staff totals at the bank were largely unchanged at just over 16,000, with personnel costs edging down to 1.7 billion marks from 1.8 billion.

Tietmeyer said it was not yet possible to predict what changes in the role and structure of the bank would emerge in the years before monetary union, when a European Central Bank will be responsible for continent-wide monetary policy.
But he said it was likely that the central bank "will have to reckon with considerably more work" during the transition to monetary union.
